examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. At nearly 450 pages, the novel is ______ : the author does not often resist the temptation to finish off a chapter, section, or even paragraph with some unnecessary flourish. (A) instructive (B) complex (C) prolix (D) educational (E) long-winded (F) explicit

solution.operation: Read the clause after the colon and state what the blank must convey: the novel is not merely long, it is padded with unnecessary flourishes
solution.result: Target meaning for the blank: excessively long because of unnecessary material
solution.description: Use the colon clause as the definition of the blank. Because the author keeps adding unnecessary flourishes, the blank must combine length with superfluity, not length alone.

solution.operation: Test 'instructive' (A) and 'educational' (D) against that target meaning
solution.result: Both eliminated: they describe instructional value, not the novel's length
solution.description: Reject these two because, whatever the novel may teach, neither word properly describes the novel's length, which is what the sentence is characterizing.

solution.operation: Test 'complex' (B) and 'explicit' (F) against the target meaning and against the same-meaning requirement
solution.result: Both eliminated: they may correlate with length but do not characterize it, and they do not yield sentences alike in meaning
solution.description: Reject these two because correlating with length is not the same as describing it, and pairing them would not produce two completed sentences that mean the same thing.

solution.result: Both mean needlessly wordy, so the two completed sentences are alike in meaning
solution.description: Confirm the surviving pair: each word carries the sense of length plus unnecessary wordiness demanded in step 1, and they are synonyms, satisfying the equivalence requirement.

examples.answer: Choice C: prolix; AND Choice E: long-winded

key_reminders: The blank must capture the whole idea signalled after the colon, here length plus unnecessary material, not just length.
Sentence Equivalence needs two words that both fit AND produce sentences alike in meaning.
A word that merely correlates with a quality does not characterize that quality.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'complex' because a 450-page novel sounds complex, though complexity is not what the colon clause describes.
Pairing the near-synonyms 'instructive' and 'educational' on synonymy alone, ignoring that they do not fit the sentence's meaning.

concept.technique_name: 4-step Critical Reasoning process for a Strengthen fill-in-the-blank

examples.problem_statement: Which of the following best completes the passage below? A nonprofit organization in Motor City has proposed that local college students be given the option to buy half-price monthly passes for the city's public transportation system. The nonprofit claims that this plan will reduce air pollution in Motor City while increasing profits for the city's public transportation system. However, this plan is unlikely to meet its goals, since ___________. (A) most college students in Motor City view public transportation as unsafe (B) most college students in Motor City view public transportation as prohibitively expensive (C) college students typically do not have the 9-to-5 schedules of most workers, and can thus be expected to ride public transportation at times when there are plenty of empty seats (D) a bus produces more air pollution per mile than does a car (E) a large proportion of the college students in Motor City live off campus

solution.operation: Identify the question: the blank at the end signals Fill in the Blank, and the word 'since' just before the blank signals a Strengthen question
solution.description: Classify the question first. 'Since' introduces a reason for the statement just made, so the right answer must support the author's claim rather than attack it.

solution.operation: Deconstruct the argument sentence by sentence: proposal (nonprofit offers half-price passes to college students) = fact; nonprofit's claim (less air pollution, more transit profit); final sentence 'this plan is unlikely to meet its goals' = the conclusion
solution.result: Conclusion: the plan will not work; the nonprofit's claim is a premise being attacked, not the conclusion
solution.description: Map the argument on paper and locate the conclusion, which in fill-in-the-blank questions sits in the final sentence. The nonprofit's claim is not labelled the conclusion for that reason.

solution.operation: State the goal: find the answer choice that gives a reason the half-price-pass plan will fail to cut pollution or raise profits
solution.result: Goal: support the author's belief that the plan will not work
solution.description: Fix the target before reading answers, so any choice that makes the plan more likely to succeed can be dismissed immediately as Reverse Logic.

solution.operation: Evaluate (A): most college students view public transportation as unsafe
solution.result: Keep: students would avoid transit even at a discount, so the plan is unlikely to succeed
solution.description: Test this choice against the goal. If students refuse to ride on safety grounds, cutting the price does not get them onto buses, which is exactly the support the author needs.

solution.operation: Evaluate (B): students view public transportation as prohibitively expensive
solution.result: Eliminate as Reverse Logic: a discount would then make them ride more, helping the plan
solution.description: Reject this choice because it identifies price as the barrier, and the plan removes half the price, so it strengthens the plan instead of undermining it.

solution.operation: Evaluate (C): students ride at off-peak times when there are plenty of empty seats
solution.result: Eliminate as Reverse Logic: filling currently empty seats is good news for transit profits
solution.description: Reject this choice because riders who fill otherwise-empty off-peak seats add revenue, supporting the profit goal rather than casting doubt on it.

solution.operation: Evaluate (D): a bus produces more air pollution per mile than a car
solution.result: Eliminate: the plan adds riders to already-running buses, and one bus can replace ten or more cars
solution.description: Reject this tempting choice by checking what the plan actually changes. No new buses are added, and per-mile comparison of one bus to one car ignores that a bus carries many car-loads of people.

solution.operation: Evaluate (E): a large proportion of students live off campus
solution.result: Eliminate as Reverse Logic: those students need transportation and might switch from cars to buses
solution.description: Reject this choice because off-campus students are precisely the ones who could shift out of cars, which would help both goals rather than hurt them.

key_reminders: 'Since' before the blank marks a Strengthen question: the answer supplies a reason for the preceding statement.
In fill-in-the-blank Critical Reasoning the conclusion is in the final sentence, not in a claim attributed to someone else.
Every problem in this set contains at least one Reverse Logic trap, an answer that helps the plan rather than hurting it.
common_mistakes: Treating the nonprofit's claim about pollution and profits as the conclusion instead of the author's 'unlikely to meet its goals'.
Falling for (D) by comparing one bus to one car, when the plan adds riders to buses already running.
Picking (B), (C), or (E), each of which supports the plan and so reverses the required direction.

concept.technique_name: contrast-signal analysis with cross-blank synonym linkage

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. While many outside the company attributed the company's success to its president's (i) ______ , insiders realized that this success owed more to the president's inflexibility than to any (ii) ______ that the president might be supposed to have displayed. Blank (i): A perseverance, B popularity, C prescience. Blank (ii): D obduracy, E caprice, F foresight.

solution.operation: Read the second half of the sentence for its contrast: the actual cause of success is the negative quality 'inflexibility', set against the quality named by Blank (ii) that outsiders supposed to be the cause
solution.result: Blank (ii) must name a positive quality, contrasted with 'inflexibility'
solution.description: Extract the contrast the sentence sets up. 'Owed more to X than to any (ii)' pits the real, negative cause against a supposed one, so Blank (ii) has to be positive.

solution.operation: Scan the Blank (ii) choices for the only positive quality among obduracy, caprice, and foresight
solution.result: 'Foresight' (Choice F) is the sole positive quality
solution.description: Apply the positive-quality requirement to the second column. Obduracy and caprice both name unfavorable traits, leaving foresight as the only fit.

solution.operation: Use the sentence's structure, in which outsiders attributed success to Blank (i) and Blank (ii) names that same supposed quality, to find the Blank (i) choice synonymous with 'foresight'
solution.result: 'Prescience' (Choice C) is the synonym of foresight, unlike perseverance or popularity
solution.description: Match the first blank to the second. Since both blanks name the quality outsiders credited, Blank (i) must mean roughly what foresight means, and only prescience does.

examples.answer: Choice C: prescience; Choice F: foresight

key_reminders: 'Owed more to inflexibility than to any (ii)' signals a contrast between a negative actual cause and a positive supposed one.
When both blanks describe the same supposed quality, the two answers must be close in meaning.
Filter the second blank first when it carries the clearer signal, then use it to constrain the first.
common_mistakes: Choosing 'obduracy' for Blank (ii) because it echoes 'inflexibility', when the blank needs the contrasting positive quality.
Selecting 'perseverance' for Blank (i) as a plausible-sounding cause of success, without checking that it matches 'foresight'.

concept.technique_name: testing candidate blank combinations for a coherent statement

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. The activists' energetic work in the service of both woman suffrage and the temperance movement in the late nineteenth century (i) ______ the assertion that the two movements were (ii) ______ . Blank (i): A undermines, B supports, C underscores. Blank (ii): D diffuse, E inimical, F predominant.

solution.operation: State what the sentence is doing: it reports what the activists' energetic work in both movements implies for some assertion about the relationship between those two movements
solution.result: Blank (i) is the implication verb; Blank (ii) fixes the content of the assertion, which is otherwise obscured
solution.description: Frame the sentence before choosing words. The two blanks are interdependent, since the verb in Blank (i) makes sense only once the assertion described by Blank (ii) is known.

solution.operation: Enumerate the two coherent readings: work in both movements could support an assertion that they were similar, or undermine an assertion that they were opposed
solution.result: Two candidate combinations, one requiring a 'similar' word in Blank (ii), the other requiring an 'opposed' word
solution.description: Reason from the evidence itself. People working energetically for both causes is evidence of compatibility, which either backs a similarity claim or damages an opposition claim.

solution.operation: Check Blank (ii) for a word meaning 'similar' or 'compatible' among diffuse, inimical, and predominant
solution.result: No such word exists, so 'supports' and the similar 'underscores' both fail
solution.description: Test the first candidate reading against the actual choices. Since nothing in the second column means similar or compatible, the supporting-verb route cannot be completed.

solution.operation: Take the remaining reading: pair 'undermines' (Choice A) with 'inimical' (Choice E), which means hostile or opposed
solution.result: 'Undermines' and 'inimical' make the only meaningful statement
solution.description: Complete the surviving combination. Evidence of activists serving both causes weakens an assertion that the movements were hostile to each other, which reads coherently, unlike the other pairings.

examples.answer: Choice A: undermines; Choice E: inimical

key_reminders: When one blank obscures the claim, generate the possible readings and test each against the available choices.
Evidence of shared participation in two movements bears on whether those movements were compatible or opposed.
If a first-blank choice has no partner in the second column, that whole reading is dead.
common_mistakes: Picking 'supports' or 'underscores' on the intuition that shared activism confirms a link, without checking that no Blank (ii) choice means 'similar'.
Treating 'underscores' and 'supports' as distinguishable here, when both fail for the same missing-partner reason.
